scenario: Today's infra track is about where data should live and when to move it once GPU memory runs out. On the inference side, VerKV keeps the full KV cache in CPU memory and fetches from it only when the error exceeds a bound. SinkState finds that linear attention states are low-rank and can stay compressed throughout. Ostinato keeps the most frequently routed experts resident in GPU memory so that short prefills of local agents can use the GPU too. On the training side, OOM plans expert execution and memory allocation together on one machine, and TRANSIT lets multi-node training use half the GPUs without changing training code. Evolving Infra decides which KV to keep based on the context state of agents.

papers.title: Dynamic Graph Indexing for Label-Filtered Approximate Nearest Neighbor Search
papers.authors: Mengxu Jiang, Zhi Yang, Fangyuan Zhang, Yin Yang, Sibo Wang
papers.abstract: Approximate nearest neighbor search (ANNS) over high-dimensional vectors is a core primitive in modern retrieval systems. In practice, objects are often also associated with labels (e.g., attributes or keywords), and retrieval must combine vector similarity with explicit label-based filtering, giving rise to label-filtered ANNS. This task is challenging because label filtering and ANNS favor very different index structures, selective filters fragment the admissible search space, and updates complicate index maintenance. To address these challenges, we propose DYLAN, a dynamic composite index for label-filtered ANNS supporting containment, overlap, and their conjunctions and disjunctions. DYLAN organizes label sets by shared prefixes in a frequency-ordered trie and selectively shares HNSW-style graph indices across trie-induced subsets, so that each trie region has a constant-factor covering index while each object participates in only logarithmically many indices. To mitigate fragmentation, DYLAN performs a cross-region multi-graph search that exploits ancestor-level indices as bridges between otherwise isolated trie regions. To support insertions, it adopts a threshold-based maintenance scheme that rebuilds shared indices only when necessary, yielding low amortized update cost. Extensive experiments with real data show that DYLAN consistently improves query throughput at comparable recall, by up to two orders of magnitude on challenging label-rich datasets, while retaining competitive memory, construction, and update costs.
papers.summary: Vector retrieval often comes with a filter, such as finding nearest neighbors only within a few tags or categories. The hard part is that once a graph index like HNSW is filtered by label, many edges get cut, qualifying points can no longer reach each other, and the search gets stuck locally. DYLAN arranges objects by their label sets in a prefix trie, builds shared graph indices on only some trie nodes, and puts each object into only logarithmically many indices. When a query spans several regions, it uses the graphs at ancestor nodes as bridges to jump between them. On YTB-Audio, a dataset with many labels, for queries that require all given labels, it is 43.5 times faster than the fastest baseline at recall of 0.95 or higher. Broken down, it visits 38.6 times fewer points than UNG, ==so the speedup comes from an index that lets the search walk less, not from low-level tuning==.

deep_reading.title: Dynamic Graph Indexing for Label-Filtered Approximate Nearest Neighbor Search

papers.title: Multi-Future Drafting: Mixture Block Drafters for Tree-Verified Speculative Decoding
papers.authors: Haoyu Huang, Jialiang Kang, Linlin Yang, Xiao Yang, Baochang Zhang
papers.abstract: Block drafters such as DFlash draft a block of future tokens in one forward pass, and draft trees such as DDTree verify the prefixes ranked highest by the product of the drafter's per-position distributions. Under tree verification, the expected number of accepted tokens is the probability mass the tree covers. We show that a product misallocates it: when the continuation can follow several futures, it splices them into chimeras, prefixes stitched together from different futures that the target never produces, and gives them as much budget as the futures themselves. Barring ties, no product-ranked tree can hold two futures that disagree in $m$ positions without $2^{m-1}-1$ chimeras, however well the drafter is trained, and in practice chimeras make up 27-33% of a 64-node tree. We propose Multi-Future Drafting (MFD), which restores the coupling with a latent variable instead of the chain rule: $K$ learned mode embeddings at the drafter's input draft $K$ coherent blocks in the same pass, and a mixture DDTree lets the verifier pick the future the target takes, losslessly and with $K+1$ extra vectors. On four Qwen targets from 4B to 27B parameters, at batch size 1, MFD reaches up to 7.8$\times$ speedup, 5-8% faster than the best single-mode tree trained identically and, on Qwen3-4B and Qwen3-8B, 9-16% faster than the released DARTree trained on the same prompts.
papers.summary: In speculative decoding, a drafter that drafts a whole block of tokens in one forward pass is fast, but it gives each position its own separate distribution. When the continuation has two equally plausible phrasings, a draft tree ranked by multiplying per-position probabilities splices them into sentences the target model would never say. The authors prove that such a tree can hold both phrasings only by also spending budget on their splices, ==and no amount of drafter training fixes it, because a product cannot express the dependence between positions==. In practice, about a third of the nodes in a 64-node tree are such splices. MFD adds K learned mode vectors at the drafter's input, drafts K internally coherent continuations side by side in the same pass, and merges them into one tree for the target to verify, leaving the output distribution unchanged. On four Qwen target models, it is 5% to 8% faster than a single-mode tree trained the same way.

deep_reading.title: Multi-Future Drafting: Mixture Block Drafters for Tree-Verified Speculative Decoding

papers.title: SinkState: On-the-Fly SVD of Recurrent States for Efficient Hybrid LLM Serving
papers.authors: Haolin Jiang, Weihang Li, Zhongzhu Zhou, Jinwen Pan, Santosh Pandey, Hang Liu
papers.abstract: Hybrid models combine softmax attention with linear attention, which compresses history into fixed-size recurrent states to balance model quality and inference efficiency. However, linear attention has not pushed this compression to its limit: we find that the queries, keys, and values of linear layers concentrate in a stable, low-dimensional subspace, a phenomenon we call the linear attention sink, so each state is effectively low-rank, with a rank that varies across states. Yet existing serving systems keep these redundant states dense, reading and rewriting them in full at every decoding step, so their memory traffic grows with the batch size and dominates the decoding cost. Thus SinkState stores each recurrent state in an adaptive low-rank form throughout inference with buffered updates and a local SVD restricted to the top subspace. SinkState further consolidates the remaining components asynchronously on the CPU. On four hybrid models with Mamba-2 and Gated DeltaNet (GDN) layers, from 4B to 120B parameters, SinkState reduces the peak memory of recurrent states by up to 2.6x (1.9x on average) and speeds up decoding by up to 1.58x (1.25x on average) over Mamba-SSM and FLA, while maintaining accuracy.
papers.summary: The linear attention layers in hybrid models compress history into a fixed-size state matrix, and every decoding step reads the whole matrix out and writes it back. With a large batch, this memory traffic takes most of the decoding time. The authors find these states are actually low-rank: the vectors that linear layers write into and read from the state sit in a small subspace that does not change with the content, and a few components recover 99% of the state. SinkState keeps every state in low-rank form throughout inference, buffers incoming updates for a few steps, runs a small SVD only on the leading components, and leaves the rest to asynchronous merging on the CPU. On four hybrid models, peak state memory drops by up to 2.6 times and decoding gets up to 1.58 times faster, with accuracy essentially unchanged. ==The states of linear attention still carry a lot of redundancy to squeeze out==, and when serving long sequences with hybrid models, the memory saved turns directly into larger batches.

deep_reading.title: SinkState: On-the-Fly SVD of Recurrent States for Efficient Hybrid LLM Serving

papers.title: Evolving Infra: Agent-Adaptive LLM Serving at Scale
papers.authors: Hao Kang, Weili Xu, Ziyang Li, Zheng Du, Hanchen Li, Tian Xia, Song Bian, Tushar Krishna, Huizi Mao, Ion Stoica, Song Han
papers.abstract: Agentic workloads are a major source of LLM inference demand. Existing prefill--decode (PD) disaggregated serving systems offer limited flexibility for runtime adaptation of compute allocation and KV cache management, and rely on coarse signals that only partly capture the diverse and dynamic agent workload. These limitations lead to load imbalance between prefill and decode nodes and eviction of KV caches that agents will reuse. We present Evolving Infra, an agent-adaptive serving framework that adapts compute allocation to agent workloads and KV cache management to agent context management at runtime. We decouple compute allocation from key--value (KV) cache management, allowing nodes to switch efficiently between prefill and decode. Building on this design, an online planner matches the PD split to workload composition, while an agent-aware distributed KV manager guides cache eviction and transfer with signals from agent context management. Across coding, math, and computer-use tasks with GLM-5.2 and Kimi K2.6 on up to 256 GB300 GPUs, Evolving Infra reduces mean end-to-end request latency and P95 TTFT by up to 4.1x and 14x over Dynamo, NVIDIA's production framework.
papers.summary: Agent workloads pose two problems for inference clusters. Some agents are prefill-heavy and others decode-heavy, and the mix drifts over time, so any fixed ratio of prefill to decode nodes loses out in some periods. Context compaction and sub-agents also change which KV is worth keeping: when a sub-agent returns after several minutes, almost the whole prompt can reuse earlier KV, while a request right after compaction can use little of it. Evicting KV by recency therefore deletes the wrong entries. Evolving Infra puts KV into a shared pool built from the host memory of all nodes, so a node can switch between prefill and decode roles without a restart and without losing its cache. An online planner adjusts the node ratio to the workload mix, and a KV manager decides what to evict first based on whether the owning agent branch is still alive. Compared with NVIDIA's Dynamo, mean end-to-end latency drops by up to 4.1 times and P95 TTFT by up to 14 times. ==When serving agents, whether a KV entry is useful depends on whether its branch is still running==.

deep_reading.title: Evolving Infra: Agent-Adaptive LLM Serving at Scale

papers.title: Verify Before You Fetch: Reliable KV Cache Compression for LLM Inference
papers.authors: Devanshu Jha, Gaurav Kumar, Agniva Chowdhury, Kumar Krishna Agrawal, Aditya Desai
papers.abstract: Long-context applications, long-lived agents, and multi-agent systems require large language models (LLMs) to process and retain extensive information. In these settings, the KV cache can exceed GPU high-bandwidth memory (HBM) capacity, necessitating offloading to host memory, where CPU-to-GPU transfers can dominate inference latency. While KV cache compression can reduce data movement, query-agnostic compression that guarantees accurate attention for arbitrary queries is extremely challenging, if not impossible. We introduce VerKV, a hybrid approach that provides $(\epsilon, \delta)$ guarantees for approximating attention on any given query. VerKV maintains a compact set of query-agnostic pivotal tokens on the GPU, together with a token-level sketch of the full KV cache, while retaining the complete cache in CPU memory. We introduce a novel stochastic sampling procedure, PoissonComp, to select the pivotal tokens. At inference time, our proposed KVFetch algorithm uses the pivotal tokens and the sketch to estimate the relative error of the resulting attention computation. If the estimate satisfies a user-specified $(\epsilon, \delta)$ tolerance, inference proceeds without accessing host memory. Otherwise, VerKV performs query-aware retrieval to fetch additional tokens from the CPU, refining the attention computation to meet the required tolerance. Thus, VerKV enables attention with bounded approximation error while minimizing CPU-to-GPU transfers. We show that PoissonComp outperforms state-of-the-art approaches to KV cache compression. Combined with KVFetch, it achieves near-dense performance (90-100% of dense quality at 32K context length, averaged over RULER and LOFT), using Qwen3-4B, Qwen3.5-9B and Ministral-3-8B, while reducing the GPU memory footprint by 8-32x and keeping CPU-to-GPU memory fetches within 2-23% of the cache per generated token, depending on the model.
papers.summary: In long-context and agent workloads, the KV cache often exceeds GPU memory and has to live in CPU memory, and moving KV back to the GPU at every step slows inference down. Keeping only a compressed KV on the GPU avoids the transfers, but gives no error guarantee, and quality collapses at high compression. VerKV keeps two things on the GPU: a small set of tokens randomly sampled by importance, and a compact summary of the full KV used to quickly estimate how relevant each token is to the current query. At each step it first uses them to estimate the error of this attention computation, computes directly if the error is within the user's tolerance, and fetches the needed tokens from the CPU only when it is not. On RULER and LOFT, with only one eighth of the KV on the GPU, it keeps 96% of full quality on average and fetches only 2% to 23% of the cache per generated token. ==The point of random sampling is that the error can be estimated, so the system knows when it must go to the CPU==.

papers.title: OOM: Offload-Optimized Full-Parameter MoE Training via Memory-Execution Co-Design
papers.authors: Ruijia Yang, Shiyuan Lin, Chengxi Liao, Zeyi Wen
papers.abstract: Offloading model state to host memory and streaming layer weights let a single multi-GPU node train large mixture-of-experts (MoE) models. GPU memory then becomes a performance budget, shared by resident expert state, retained activations, and execution worksets. The best allocation depends on the expert execution path, batch size, and sequence length. We present OOM (Offload-Optimized MoE), a full-parameter MoE training system that co-designs expert execution and memory allocation. For expert-parallel execution, OOM updates resident experts on their owning GPUs and jointly plans state residency and MoE activation retention according to pipeline dependencies. For local execution, OOM bounds GPU worksets through dependency-aware partitioning; in hybrid models, it also retains attention results on the host to avoid costly recomputation and selectively regenerates layer boundaries through cheaper layers to make room. Calibrated cost models guide joint configuration within GPU and host budgets to minimize step time; OOM selects among the configured paths through short executions. On four H100s, OOM trains with 1M-token contexts, whereas FSDP2, ZeRO-Offload, and MegaTrain exhaust GPU memory at 512K. It also trains a 122B-parameter MoE model, on which all three exhaust host memory. On four 24 GB RTX 4090s, it trains 512K-token contexts and 1,024 1K-token sequences per step without gradient accumulation. Across matched-global-batch comparisons, OOM delivers 1.58x and 4.08x geometric-mean (up to 2.14x and 7.77x) throughput over CPU-offloaded FSDP2 on the two platforms while using the least host memory among the evaluated systems -- as little as 1/3.0 of FSDP2's.
papers.summary: With model state in CPU memory and weights streamed into the GPU layer by layer, a single multi-GPU machine can train a large MoE with full parameters. GPU memory then becomes a budget to divide, contested by resident expert parameters, retained activations and temporary compute space, and the split directly decides how fast a training step runs. OOM plans expert execution and memory allocation together, using calibrated cost models plus short trial runs to pick the fastest configuration between expert parallelism and computing all experts locally on each GPU. ==Change how memory is split and the faster execution path can flip==, so the two decisions have to be made together. On four H100s it trains with 1M-token contexts, while FSDP2 and the other baselines run out of GPU memory at 512K. Its throughput averages 1.58 times that of CPU-offloaded FSDP2, while using the least host memory.

papers.title: Ostinato: Fast CPU-GPU MoE Inference for Local Agents via Resident Experts in Every Forward Pass
papers.abstract: Language-model agents increasingly run on workstations with a few consumer GPUs, where large mixture-of-experts (MoE) models keep part of their experts in host memory. With existing CPU-GPU engines, these agents get fast prefill or fast decode, not both: llama.cpp's expert cache skips forward passes of more than 32 tokens to keep the experts of decode cached, so an agent waits 2.1-2.8 s after each tool output, whereas its default layer placement shortens this wait but is 1.5-1.6$\times$ slower in decode. Our key insight is that a short prefill touches too many distinct experts to upload, yet sends 84% of its expert activations (routes) to a stable set of experts that fits in GPU memory. We present Ostinato, a CPU-GPU MoE inference engine that computes these experts on the GPUs in every forward pass without changing what the model computes. Short prefills split their routes, leaving fewer than one of a token's six routed experts per layer to the CPU; long prefills upload each distinct cold expert once; and each decode step runs as one fixed-shape CUDA graph per GPU. On real coding and customer-service agent sessions with DeepSeek-V4-Flash on four RTX 4090D GPUs, Ostinato is the fastest engine in both phases and finishes every session sooner than all six baselines. Against llama.cpp and KTransformers, it cuts the median wait after a tool output by 22-55% and finishes sessions 1.4-2.5$\times$ sooner.
papers.summary: When a large MoE model runs an agent locally on a few consumer GPUs, the experts do not fit, and part of them must stay in CPU memory. Existing engines force a choice: either decode is fast but the short prefill after each tool output cannot use the experts in GPU memory, so the agent sits waiting for over two seconds, or prefill is fast and decode is noticeably slower. The authors observe that a short prefill touches many distinct experts, yet the routes its tokens actually take are concentrated: the 44% of experts used most in development sessions receive 84% of the routes in new sessions. Ostinato keeps these experts resident in GPU memory and computes them on the GPU in every forward pass, prefill or decode, while cold experts go to the CPU and the model's outputs stay unchanged. On DeepSeek-V4-Flash, it finishes whole agent sessions up to 2.5 times sooner than existing engines. ==Counted by routes instead of by distinct experts, even a short prefill is worth computing on the GPU==.

papers.title: Why Kubernetes Cannot Contain a Full Lazy-Pulling Cache: Two Impossibility Results and a Bounded, Honest Design for Model Serving
papers.abstract: Lazy container-image pulling makes cold starts of autoscaled model-serving fleets on Kubernetes nearly independent of model size, but it moves the model's bytes into a node-level cache that the platform neither bounds nor accounts for. This article establishes, by experiment, two impossibility results for that cache. A monitoring-side remedy cannot catch its failure: a sentinel readiness probe stays green while 272 of 280 files are unreadable. A platform-side remedy cannot contain it: kubelet, given full disk-pressure visibility, frees 0 bytes and evicts 26 bystander pods, because its reclamation actuator is keyed to an accounting that does not know the cache exists. The article then eliminates the failure class inside the component that owns the bytes, with no change to kubelet or the container runtime interface, by two design rules: a byte budget whose pressure signal is keyed to filesystem truth, so that a never-blocking, lossy accounting still enforces a hard bound (held against about 301,000 dropped updates), and pass-through semantics under which a failed cache write never becomes a failed read, with the coupling traced to a single llama.cpp. Across six pre-specified campaigns on AWS, upstream stargz-snapshotter fails 273 of 280 model files at 90% cache pre-fill; the proposed system reads all 150.3 GB with zero errors at +18.5% completion cost and holds the budget under a live read, co-tenancy, and a three-node fleet. A source audit shows the missing bound generalizes to SOCI and Nydus. The implementation is open source and has been proposed upstream.
papers.summary: Lazy image pulling on Kubernetes makes cold starts of model serving almost independent of model size, at the cost of writing the model's bytes into a node-level cache that has no quota and that the platform does not account for. Once the cache fills, Pods already serving start failing to read their model files while health checks all stay green. The authors show by experiment that neither of the two remedies an operator has works. A readiness check that reads a few sentinel files still reports healthy while 272 of 280 files are unreadable. Kubernetes sees the disk pressure yet frees not a single byte, and instead evicts a group of unrelated Pods, because its reclamation has no idea the cache exists. ==The problem can only be fixed inside the component that actually holds the bytes==. The authors give the cache a hard byte budget triggered by actual disk usage, and when a cache write fails the data is still handed to the reader, just not kept. After the change every model file can be read, at 18.5% more completion time.

papers.title: OverlapAdvisor: Modeling and Adapting Computation-Communication Overlap for Distributed MoE Serving
papers.authors: Chutong Ding, Kaixuan Zhang, Luping Wang, Shiyou Qian, Jian Cao, Cheng Huang, Guodong Yang, Liping Zhang
papers.abstract: Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) inference with expert parallelism (EP) relies on All-to-All communication, making computation-communication overlap strategies critical for achieving high performance. However, no strategy is universally optimal. Across 103 production configurations, varying input lengths, and four hardware platforms, we observe that the fastest strategy shifts based on model shape, EP degree, input length, and hardware. Since no strategy dominates more than 80.6% of configurations, configuration-aware selection is necessary. In this work, we propose OverlapAdvisor, which models overlap stages using two granularities to capture computation-communication dependencies. OverlapAdvisor builds a unified performance model, accounting for deviations from peak compute, memory, and communication performance across workloads and hardware. This model enables launch-time, configuration-aware strategy selection within two serving engines. We conduct experiments on four MoE models (30B-235B) against three baselines, utilizing SGLang and vLLM. At the kernel level, OverlapAdvisor achieves 1.16x average and 1.59x maximum speedups, with a prediction MAPE of 3.3%-15.9%. In SGLang and vLLM, it improves end-to-end throughput up to 31.7%. Its granularity-guided optimizations further achieve median speedups of 1.10x for DeepEP-v1 and 1.22x for FlashMoE.
papers.summary: In MoE inference with expert parallelism, tokens are sent to experts on different GPUs through All-to-All, and there are already several ways to overlap this communication with computation, such as Comet, FlashMoE and DeepEP. The authors test them all under the same conditions on 103 production MoE shapes, input lengths from decode to long prefill, and four GPU platforms, and find that none wins everywhere, with even the best one fastest in only 80.6% of configurations. OverlapAdvisor uses one unified performance model to estimate how long each approach takes under a given configuration, accounting for how far real bandwidth and compute fall short of peak, and picks the fastest one when the server launches, without running benchmarks on the spot. In SGLang and vLLM, end-to-end throughput improves by up to 31.7%. ==The overlap strategy should be chosen by model shape, expert-parallel degree and input length==, and sticking to one always loses on some configurations.

papers.title: TRANSIT: Transparent Scale-in for Multi-Node LLM Training
papers.authors: Hyungyo Kim, Nicholas Satchanov, Hrishi Shah, Gaohan Ye, Jiaqi Lou, Robert Walkup, Shweta Salaria, I-Hsin Chung, Hubertus Franke, Seetharami Seelam, Apoorve Mohan, Nam Sung Kim
papers.abstract: TRANSIT is a transparent scale-in framework to enable multi-node model training on fewer GPUs while maintaining training efficiency by transparently leveraging CPU DRAM as an extension of GPU memory during distributed training. It achieves this through a user-space interposition layer, requiring no modifications to the application, training framework, cluster scheduler, device driver, or operating system. Furthermore, TRANSIT achieves higher efficiency by leveraging a zero-copy data path for CPU-GPU transfers. We evaluate TRANSIT on dense and MoE models across scales up to 64 NVIDIA H100 GPUs and multiple parallelism configurations over a RoCE network. Our evaluation shows that TRANSIT can: (a) outperform state-of-the-art framework-managed offloading techniques, achieving up to 68%, 59%, and 42% higher per-GPU throughput than TorchTitan, ZeRO-Offload, and ZeRO-Infinity, respectively, (b) enables training with 50% fewer GPUs while maintaining over 90% of baseline per-GPU throughput, (c) lower per-node network traffic by up to 33%, and (d) improve per-GPU throughput by up to 35% in communication-bound settings.
papers.summary: LLM training often adds machines only to get enough GPU memory, but more machines mean more participants in collective communication and more network congestion. TRANSIT goes the other way, using CPU memory to extend GPU memory so the same training job runs on fewer GPUs. It intercepts all GPU memory allocations in user space and redirects them to unified virtual memory, with no changes to the training code, framework, scheduler or driver. Relying on unified virtual memory's default page-fault migration would be slow, so TRANSIT keeps frequently reused activations and half-precision parameters in GPU memory, while rarely used data such as optimizer states is read by the GPU directly from host memory without being copied in. On an H100 cluster, it keeps over 90% of per-GPU throughput with half the GPUs, and its per-GPU throughput is up to 59% higher than ZeRO-Offload's. ==Fewer machines means fewer participants in communication, so network congestion matters less==.
